name: Shivaji
role: Founder and first Chhatrapati of the Maratha kingdom (r. 1674-1680)
summary: Shivaji founded a sovereign Maratha kingdom and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. He directed a council of eight ministers, used military campaigns to extend his territory and collect tribute, and maintained state support for Hindu and Muslim places of worship.

sources.title: Shivaji and His Times (2nd ed., 1920), full text
sources.author: Jadunath Sarkar
sources.usedFor: Coronation, administration, army orders (Sabhasad), religious policy, raids, succession

sources.title: Siva Chhatrapati, Sabhasad Bakhar, English translation (1920)
sources.author: Krishnaji Anant Sabhasad, translated and edited by Surendra Nath Sen
sources.usedFor: The 1697 court chronicle, especially territorial campaigns, the coronation, land assessment, religious endowments and military administration.

sources.title: Who Was Shivaji? (English translation), pp. 19–20
sources.author: Govind Pansare
sources.usedFor: Shivaji’s customs order on imported salt reported in the section on protection of trade and industry.

sources.title: English Records on Shivaji (1659–1682), Henry Oxinden’s embassy journal, entry of 8 June 1674 (Rare Books Society of India scan)
sources.author: Henry Oxinden, published by Shivcharitra Karyalaya
sources.usedFor: Contemporary report of Shivaji’s fourth marriage, in the journal of the English envoy at Raigad.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Shivaji publicly recognized his son as crown prince and grounded his own coronation rites in an officially recognized Kshatriya lineage.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Shivaji organized direct paid service in his military and civil administration. Sabhasad describes treasury salaries for officers and troops and the hiring of horsemen with their own mounts.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: After the 1665 Treaty of Purandar transferred forts to Mughal control, Shivaji resumed war and took back several forts held by Mughal garrisons in his former territories.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: In the 1664 raid on Mughal Surat, Shivaji deliberately targeted civilian merchants to extract wealth. Sarkar records his order to mutilate a merchant who could not produce cash.

clerical-rule.rationale: Shivaji held sovereign authority himself and assigned the Pandit Rao responsibility for ecclesiastical affairs within the royal administration.

destroy-worshipped-objects.rationale: Shivaji maintained state allowances for Hindu temples and Muslim shrines and mosques. Sabhasad records funding for illumination and offerings at places of worship.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Shivaji installed himself as sovereign at his 1674 coronation and presented his son as heir to the crown.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Shivaji seated his son Sambhaji as crown prince at the 1674 coronation, publicly designating his child as heir to the throne.

elective-rulers.rationale: Shivaji instituted a monarchy and publicly designated his own son as crown prince at the coronation.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Shivaji’s regulations assigned different fort offices by birth caste, reserving two posts for Marathas and another for Brahmans. His campaign rules also exempted Brahmans from being held for ransom.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: Shivaji made repeated armed levies in neighbouring states a routine policy and installed his own garrisons and administration in annexed parts of the Karnatak.

head-commands-forces.rationale: As sovereign he commanded the army personally and appointed his eight ministers (ashta pradhan), who in Sarkar's account acted as his advisers and secretaries while he kept administration in his own hands.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: Shivaji maintained a state cavalry and used animals for military transport. Sabhasad reports that campaign orders allowed troops to seize bullocks for transport.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: Shivaji routinely sent troops into neighbouring territory to collect tribute by force and used his army to annex parts of the Karnatak.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Shivaji appointed a chief justice to decide cases according to Sanskrit Hindu law books, which supplied rules for civil and criminal adjudication.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Shivaji made annual expeditions to exact contributions from neighbouring territories a regular purpose of his army. Sabhasad describes the campaign cycle and the collection of booty and tribute.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Shivaji’s coronation established him as the governing sovereign. The record gives no position on a hereditary monarch whose duties are ceremonial.

more-religion-public.rationale: Shivaji made the Pandit Rao a state officer responsible for religious affairs and used state revenue to support temples, mosques and religious scholars.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Shivaji used public revenue to maintain shrines and support religious scholars. His revenue administration also provided seed and cattle advances to new cultivators.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Shivaji contracted multiple publicly recognized royal marriages while existing wives were alive. The English envoy Henry Oxinden recorded his fourth marriage in the journal entry for 8 June 1674.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: Shivaji assigned his ministers an advisory role and reserved policy decisions to himself, as Sarkar describes in chapter XV.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Shivaji appointed a chief justice to hear civil and criminal cases and oversee judicial decisions throughout the kingdom.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Pandit Rao had authority over impiety, heresy and penance. The sources do not identify a criminal prohibition on publicly insulting sacred beliefs or objects.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Shivaji ordered Sanskrit titles for his ministers in place of Persian ones. That order concerned the names of offices and gives no position on eliminating loanwords from the language as a whole.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Shivaji broke with Bijapur’s rule and displaced its authority with his own sovereign government, holding the territories he conquered under an independent crown.

separate-church-state.rationale: Shivaji vested the Pandit Rao with public authority over religious ceremonies, doctrine and caste disputes. His administration also funded Hindu and Muslim shrines.

separated-powers.rationale: Shivaji appointed and directed the eight ministers personally. Sarkar describes the council as advisory, with the king retaining control of policy and administration.

state-harmful.rationale: Shivaji established a sovereign government, appointed ministers and judges, and organized military and revenue administrations for the territory he ruled.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Shivaji used state allowances to sustain learned religious practitioners, including Vedic scholars and ascetics, and to maintain places of worship.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Pansare reports that Shivaji instructed Narhari Anandrao in 1671 to impose a heavy duty on imported salt to prevent outside traders from displacing local producers.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Shivaji annexed territory in his southern campaign and installed Maratha garrisons in conquered forts, including Jinji and Vellore. Sarkar describes the annexed region and its administration in chapter XV.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: Sarkar reproduces the English chaplain’s account of Shivaji’s treatment of prisoners at Surat in 1664, including whipping and mutilation to force disclosures. He reports Shivaji personally ordering such punishment.

notes: This pass checked government and liberty against the coronation, council and judicial offices, succession and the Surat prisoner accounts. It checked world affairs and political means against the campaigns, the Purandar settlement, diplomatic correspondence in House of Shivaji, and the English factory records. It checked the economy against the land assessment, advances to cultivators, cash pay, customs and commercial negotiations, and reviewed society and culture against religious endowments, official terminology and the royal marriages. For ecology, technology and globalism it checked the evidence on animal transport, timber, shipbuilding and cross-border commerce. The timber rule often attributed to Shivaji is transmitted in the later Ajnapatra and was excluded as his own evidence. Specific measures on farm credit, official titles and Dutch slave trading did not settle the adjacent broader statements. The letter against jizya is preserved in Sarkar’s translation with disputed attribution and is superseded on legal equality by the caste distinctions in the administrative and military record. Village adjudication was checked against Sarkar’s account of local fact-finding juries and the royal chief justice. The record did not establish a general rule of subsidiarity, minority autonomy, secession or minority-language support. The late-seventeenth-century Sabhasad chronicle is used as an account of the record. The surviving evidence covers too few of the current dividing lines.
